prompt: In Spolsky's argument, why does old code look ugly?
hint: Each odd branch has a history.

choices.text: It was written in a hurry by people who left
choices.why: Haste happens, and it is not his point: the ugliness he means is the trace of fixes.

choices.text: Its odd branches are fixes for bugs met in production
choices.why: Right: the special cases are knowledge nobody wrote down elsewhere, and a rewrite throws them away.

choices.text: Languages and frameworks have moved on since it was written
choices.why: Fashion ages code's look, but Spolsky's claim is about what the code contains.

choices.text: Nobody has been allowed to refactor it
choices.why: Permission is not the issue; refactoring keeps the fixes, which is why it is safer than starting again.

prompt: Match each reason rewrites fail to what it costs.
hint: The lesson closes with this table.

pairs.left: The knowledge lives in the old code

pairs.right: A scope that grows past any estimate
A finish line that recedes, or a business that waits
Every risk landing on a single cutover

prompt: The second page of Mateus's proposal adds an event bus, venue plugins and selling outside Brazil. Which failure does that show?

choices.text: The moving target
choices.why: The moving target is the old system changing; this is the new one growing.

choices.text: Value only at the end
choices.why: That one is about when the rewrite pays; these additions are about how big it gets.

choices.text: Knowledge that lives in the old code
choices.why: That failure loses old behaviour; these lines add behaviour nobody asked for.

choices.text: The second-system effect
choices.why: Right: confident designers put in everything held back the first time, and the estimate stops meaning anything.

prompt: To stop the moving target, a company freezes its old system for the eighteen months of a rewrite. By the lesson, what has it bought, and at what price?
hint: The choice is unpleasant either way.

choices.text: A fixed target; the business waits a year and a half
choices.why: Right: freezing removes one failure by creating the other half of the same dilemma.

choices.text: A safe rewrite, since the other three failures depend on the target moving
choices.why: Hidden requirements, a growing scope and a single cutover all remain with the target fixed.

choices.text: Nothing, because a frozen system keeps changing through hotfixes anyway
choices.why: Some fixes will slip in, but the freeze does slow the target; the lesson's objection is its cost to the business.

choices.text: A cheaper rewrite, since engineers move from the old system to the new
choices.why: Moving people changes who pays, not the cost; the rewrite's hours are the same.

prompt: Fred Brooks's name for a designer putting into the next version everything held back the first time is the ___ effect.
What are the two halves of the lesson's first case for a rewrite?
hint: A size and a way back.

choices.text: A senior team and a written design
choices.why: Neither changes the failures; the conditions are about size and reversibility, not the team.

choices.text: A modern stack and a lower cloud bill
choices.why: Those are reasons people give for wanting a rewrite, not conditions that make one safe.

choices.text: Fits within a quarter, and the cutover is reversible
choices.why: Right: small enough that the target barely moves, and reversible so a mistake costs a morning.

choices.text: Approved by the CTO and paid for from the debt budget
choices.why: Approval and budget decide whether it happens, not whether the four failures apply.

prompt: Which of these are the second case, the ground going away? Choose all that apply.
hint: Doing nothing has stopped being an option.

choices.text: Its runtime stops receiving security fixes
choices.why: Yes: Python 2 is the lesson's example; the foundation is ending.

choices.text: The vendor of the platform a component runs on closes it
choices.why: Yes: there is no staying put, only a choice between ways of moving.

choices.text: The code is nine years old and hard to read
choices.why: Age and ugliness describe the reservation module, and nothing under it is ending.

choices.text: A newer framework has become the popular choice
choices.why: Popularity does not take the old foundation away; the old one keeps working.

prompt: Why does Mateus's reservation rewrite meet neither case?
hint: Run it through the table's three questions.

choices.text: The team proposing it is too small for a monolith
choices.why: Team size is not one of the questions; a bigger team would not make the cutover reversible.

choices.text: Eighteen months, one switch, nothing beneath it ending
choices.why: Right: too big for a quarter, irreversible, and its foundation is not going away.

choices.text: The seat-hold code has already been moved out of it
choices.why: That move is lesson 7, and it is the alternative to the rewrite rather than a reason against it.

choices.text: Rails is a poor fit for a ticketing platform at this scale
choices.why: The lesson makes no claim about Rails; the verdict comes from size, reversibility and the foundation.

prompt: A team will rewrite a small pricing component in two weeks. The cutover converts every stored price to a new format, and the old format cannot be restored. How does the lesson judge it?
hint: Both halves of the condition matter.

choices.text: Case one: two weeks fits easily inside a quarter
choices.why: That is only one half; with no way back it is still a big-bang cutover.

choices.text: Case two: the old price format is going away
choices.why: The team is removing that format by choice; case two is a foundation ending whether you act or not.

choices.text: Small but irreversible: a big-bang cutover, only at a smaller scale
choices.why: Right: small without reversible still puts every risk on one morning; keeping a way back is what is missing.

choices.text: Fine, as long as the team runs a load test before the cutover
choices.why: A load test checks capacity, not correctness, and it does not make the conversion undoable.

prompt: Put the steps for judging a rewrite proposal in the order the lesson gives them.
hint: Start with the cheap case; the forced case comes second.
items: Ask whether it fits within a quarter and can be undone
If not, ask whether the ground under the old system is going away
If it is, look for a path that moves it one piece at a time
Only when no such path exists, rewrite
trap: Jumping to the rewrite as soon as the ground is going away skips the incremental path, which the lesson says to look for first even in case two.

prompt: A smaller rewrite is proposed: 4 engineers for 12 months, at 160 hours a month each. How many hours does it cost?
hint: Engineers × months × hours a month, as in the sheet.

prompt: With the 1.5× overrun the rewrite costs 25,920 hours and still saves 120 hours a sprint once shipped. How many sprints does it take to pay back?
hint: Hours divided by hours saved a sprint.

prompt: The proposal pays back in 5.5 years. Why does the lesson say the money is back about seven years after the first commit?

choices.text: Interest rates on borrowed money add the gap
choices.why: No money is borrowed here; the gap is time spent building with nothing saved.

choices.text: Saving starts only when it ships, after 18 months
choices.why: Right: 1.5 years of building, then 5.5 years of payback, and the old interest is paid in full meanwhile.

choices.text: The engineers' hourly rate rises during the rewrite
choices.why: The rate is fixed at R$ 150 throughout the sheet.

choices.text: A 1.5× overrun is built into the proposal's own plan
choices.why: The overrun is Davi's test, not the proposal's plan; with it the wait is more than ten years.

prompt: The proposal's saving of 120 hours a sprint is more than twice anything measured. Why did Davi put it in the sheet anyway?

choices.text: He believed it, since nobody had measured the rest
choices.why: He calls it generous; an unmeasured remainder is a reason for doubt, not for belief.

choices.text: The CFO asked for the most optimistic case first
choices.why: Otávio is not part of this exchange; the sheet answers Mateus's proposal.

choices.text: A smaller saving would have made the sheet too complex
choices.why: Any number divides the same way; the choice of number was about the argument, not the arithmetic.

choices.text: It still holds with the other side's best number
choices.why: Right: if the rewrite fails to pay with its own claim, nobody can say the sheet was rigged against it.

prompt: When Davi applies a 1.5× overrun, what changes in the sum?
hint: Look at the saving row in the table.

choices.text: Cost grows by half; the saving stays at R$ 18,000
choices.why: Right: an overrun adds cost and time and nothing to the saving, so the payback stretches to 8.3 years.

choices.text: Cost and saving both grow by half, so payback stays put
choices.why: A late system saves nothing extra for being late; only the cost grows.

choices.text: Only the months change; the cost stays at R$ 2,592,000
choices.why: Longer means more hours of six people, so the cost rises to R$ 3,888,000.

choices.text: The saving drops, as the old system ages further
choices.why: The sheet keeps the saving at 120 hours a sprint in both columns.

prompt: The Data team proposes rewriting its export job in six weeks. The old job keeps running, and a setting picks which one sends each night's files. How does the lesson judge it?
hint: Check both halves of the first case.

choices.text: Refuse it, since Spolsky's rule is not to rewrite
choices.why: The lesson calls that reading too strong; the failures have conditions, and this proposal removes them.

choices.text: Reasonable: small, and reversible by a setting
choices.why: Right: it is case one, the same shape as the PDF generator.

choices.text: Accept it only if the export job's foundation is ending
choices.why: That is case two; case one does not need it.

choices.text: Run it as a strangler migration over twelve months
choices.why: A six-week job with a switch back needs no year-long migration; lesson 7's method is for what cannot be rewritten safely.

prompt: The rewrite as proposed costs R$ 2,592,000; the seat-hold debt's principal is R$ 48,000. How many times the principal is the rewrite?
What was Davi's answer to Mateus?
hint: No to one thing, yes to part of it.

choices.text: Yes, once the overrun is in the plan
choices.why: With the overrun the payback is 8.3 years; adding it to the plan makes the case weaker.

choices.text: Not this year, as microservices wait a year in the strategy
choices.why: The strategy does delay microservices, but Davi's reply rests on the sum, and it moves the seat-hold code now.

choices.text: A rewrite of the seat-hold module alone, in eighteen months
choices.why: Moving the seat-hold code is the answer, but one piece at a time while sales go on, not as a rewrite.

choices.text: No to the rewrite; yes to moving seat holds out now
choices.why: Right: the part that hurts gets moved without stopping the sales, which is lesson 7.

prompt: Davi lists where the rewrite sum is generous to the rewrite. Which of these are on that list? Choose all that apply.
hint: Generous means the real number is likely worse for the rewrite.

choices.text: A 120-hour saving, over twice what was measured
choices.why: Yes: it is the proposal's own claim, and lesson 5 measured 55 hours on the named debts.

choices.text: No cost for features built twice, once in each system
choices.why: Yes: the moving target has a price, and the sheet leaves it out.

choices.text: The cost of the six engineers' hours at R$ 150
choices.why: That cost is in the sum; it is the R$ 2,592,000.

choices.text: No credit for anything new the system could do
choices.why: That is the list in the other direction, where the sheet is unfair to the rewrite.
